title: Drennan v. Star Paving Co.
summary: A subcontractor’s definite bid that the general contractor foreseeably and reasonably relied on in submitting its own bid became irrevocable, under § 90, long enough to give the general a reasonable chance to accept after the award; the subcontractor’s unnoticed mistake did not excuse it, and the general recovered the difference between the bid and the replacement cost.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of California (1958).

The court’s use of § 45 is analogical. The assigned note connects the case to § 87(2). The replacement-price award is not proof that every reliance-based action receives expectation damages.

sections.Parties: William A. Drennan, a licensed general contractor, was the plaintiff and respondent; he sought the extra cost of paving after the subcontractor refused to perform at its quoted price. Star Paving Company was the defendant and appellant, maintaining that its bid was a revocable offer withdrawn before acceptance. The Lancaster school district, which awarded Drennan the main contract, was not a party.
sections.Material Facts: On July 28, 1955 Drennan prepared a bid for the Monte Vista school project in Lancaster, due before 8 p.m. As was customary, subcontractors telephoned their quotations on bidding day; his secretary took fifty to seventy-five. Late that afternoon Star’s estimator quoted $7,131.60 for the paving and repeated the figure while Drennan listened on an extension. It was the lowest paving bid; Drennan used it to compute his total of $317,385, named Star as paving subcontractor as the bidding rules required for subcontractors doing at least half a percent of the work, and posted a ten percent bid bond. He won the contract. The next morning, before he had communicated acceptance, Star’s engineer said the bid was a mistake and could not be honored for less than $15,000. Drennan insisted on performance and, after months seeking replacement bids, hired L & H Paving for $10,948.60.
sections.Procedural History: Drennan sued Star for the additional paving cost. The trial court found that Star had made a definite offer to do the specified work for $7,131.60, that Drennan relied on it in computing his bid and naming Star, and that he had no reason to know of the mistake; it awarded $3,817, the difference between the bid and the reasonable replacement cost, plus costs. Star appealed, arguing that no consideration supported an option, that using the bid formed no bilateral contract, and that it withdrew before acceptance; it also pleaded mistake and attacked the damages allegations. The Supreme Court of California, Justice Traynor writing for a unanimous court, affirmed on December 31, 1958.
sections.Issue: Did Drennan’s foreseeable and reasonable reliance on Star’s definite subcontract bid make the offer temporarily irrevocable, even though he had neither paid for an option nor accepted before Star tried to withdraw? Could Star escape because its bid resulted from mistake, and did Drennan adequately show mitigation and damages?
sections.Holding: Yes. Reasonable, foreseeable reliance producing a prejudicial change of position can support an implied subsidiary promise not to revoke an offer, without bargained-for consideration. Under § 90 of the First Restatement, Star’s bid became irrevocable long enough to give Drennan a reasonable opportunity to accept after the general contract was awarded; using the figure was not itself an acceptance, but reliance protected his later chance to accept. Star’s mistake did not defeat recovery because Drennan had no reason to know of it and had already committed himself, and the evidence showed reasonable mitigation. The $3,817 judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Star had not bargained for Drennan’s use of its bid in exchange for a promise to keep it open, and using the bid did not bind Drennan to award Star the subcontract, so there was neither a paid option nor a bilateral contract. Section 90 supplied the answer. Star submitted its bid to win the subcontract and could expect a low bid to be used in Drennan’s computation and help him win the award. Once Drennan committed himself to the owner at a price built on Star’s figure, fairness required protecting a reasonable opportunity to accept. Section 45’s protection of an offeree who begins the performance a unilateral offer invites supplied an analogy: an implied subsidiary promise keeps the offer open, and foreseeable preacceptance reliance justified comparable protection. The protection has limits: a general contractor may not delay acceptance while shopping for a better price or reopen bargaining while holding the bid in reserve,. Mistake did not shift the loss, because Drennan lacked notice of error and paving quotations varied by as much as 160 percent. Months of seeking quotations satisfied mitigation.

sections.Parties: General contractor Drennan sued subcontractor Star Paving.
sections.Material Facts: Drennan used Star’s paving bid in his successful general bid. Star then claimed a pricing mistake and refused to perform at the bid price; replacement performance cost more.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded Drennan the additional replacement cost. The California Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could Star revoke after Drennan reasonably relied on the bid but before acceptance was communicated?
sections.Holding: The reliance supplied a basis for holding the offer open for a reasonable opportunity to accept.
sections.Reasoning: Star should reasonably have expected its bid to be used in the general bid. Drennan’s reliance was reasonable, and the circumstances justified protection against revocation.

priorVersions.summary: Reasonable reliance on a subcontractor’s bid made it temporarily irrevocable without itself constituting acceptance of the subcontract.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Supreme Court of California (1958).

Do not collapse irrevocability into acceptance. The notes’ Holman decision likewise rejects automatic acceptance merely from using and listing a subcontractor’s bid. The negligence discussion is an alternative possibility considered by the opinion, not the basis actually adjudicated.

sections.Parties: Drennan, a general contractor, sued Star Paving, the subcontractor that submitted a paving bid.
sections.Material Facts: Star quoted $7,131.60 for the Monte Vista school paving work shortly before general bids were due. Drennan used it in a $317,385 bid, named Star, and provided the required bid bond. After Drennan won, Star announced an estimating mistake and demanded at least $15,000. Drennan promptly insisted on the original bid and ultimately hired another paver for $10,848.60.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded the $3,717 difference. The Supreme Court of California affirmed. The assigned introduction contrasts James Baird, and the following notes address preparations, reciprocal obligations, and the later Restatement § 87(2).
sections.Issue: Could the subcontractor revoke before communicated acceptance when it had reason to expect the general contractor to rely on its bid?
sections.Holding: The reliance supported an implied subsidiary promise not to revoke, giving the general contractor a reasonable opportunity to accept after award of the main contract. The court sustained the damages award.
sections.Reasoning: Using the bid was neither an acceptance binding both parties nor consideration for an expressly bargained-for option. Section 90 supplied a reliance-based reason to hold the offer open. The court analogized to § 45’s protection for beginning invited performance, without treating this bid as a performance-only offer. Star expected and wanted the bid used. Drennan’s commitment to the owner made withdrawal prejudicial. Known or reasonably apparent error would defeat justified reliance, while the range of bids here did not put Drennan on such notice. The general contractor could not delay to shop for a better deal or reopen bargaining and still insist on a continuing option.

learning.why: Drennan connects promissory estoppel with revocation: reliance can keep a subcontractor’s offer open even though no bilateral subcontract has yet formed. Contrast James Baird and the distinct protection for beginning invited performance under Restatement § 45.

topics.option-contracts: The result protects an opportunity to accept without finding a paid option.
